paragraphs: “Malika! Malika! Come on, we’re going to be late, I don’t want to be late again!”

Ten-year-old Malika, still half-asleep, chewed her msemen slowly, the flaky layered pancake prepared by her Algerian grandmother every day. Her gidda, her grandma, filled the msemen with a bit of egg mixed with light brown sugar. When she cooked the pancake in olive oil, their small two-bedroom apartment smelled like caramel. It was the only smell in the world that could get Malika out of her bed at 7 a.m. to prepare for school, one block away from their social housing in Septèmes-les-Vallons, a small town sandwiched between Marseille and the wealthy Pennes Mirabeau. Malika wiped her fingers on the napkin. Her grandmother had her greyish hair wrapped in a flowery hijab. She wore a colorful dress with giant green and yellow flowers spreading across her small chest and shoulders. Her gidda was barely taller than Malika who had outpaced even the boys in her class. Malika’s mother worked as a caretaker in the psychiatric hospital of Edouard Toulouse, a somber place that sent shivers through Malika whenever she visited, which happened rarely. Two or three years ago, gidda had to stay at a nearby hospital for nearly two weeks because of her high blood pressure. Malika’s mother had to take her to Edouard Toulouse when she didn’t have school. Malika shook her head to avoid thinking about this time. Her gidda was fine now. That’s what she told herself when she looked at the smiling woman who now looked a bit stressed as the clock continued to click down and brought them closer to 8 a.m., when school started.

Gidda walked up to Malika, took a napkin and wiped the flaky pastry bits that had stuck at the corners of her granddaughter’s mouth. The child looked so much like her father. Her mouth and eyes were the same. He had died from cancer when she was just three years old. Gidda had moved in with her daughter to help her out. Gidda’s husband had died in an accident, a factory one, back in Algeria where the family was from. Mektoub, destiny, Gidda told herself. “God knows best, He is Great,” she muttered to herself.
Malika sat in the middle rows of her classroom. She watched the teacher, a stocky brunette called Miss Lauret, write a few words in English on the blackboard. Malika loved learning languages.

At home, her gidda spoke to her mother in the brisk Arabic of Algeria, derija. French words popped in their sentences like funny clowns, an automobile transformed itself in tomobile and telephone became tiliphone. Her gidda also sang when she cooked. She spoke soft words of Tamazight, her indigenous language from Kabylia where the fig and olive trees cast their shadows on mounds of semolina cakes made gooey by honey, or at least that’s how Malika imagined the place based on her gidda’s stories.
Malika learned: U-N-I-T-E-D K-I-N-G-D-O-M. A strange country made of other nations located even further up North than Paris, which for her was the northernmost place in the world.

Miss Lauret projected a map of the United Kingdom and indicated the nations that made up this country. Malika dreamed of another map, of a country further down, Algeria, and pictured Miss Lauret pointing to her Kabylia and to Algiers, which she had visited once when she was seven years old.

The bell roused her, it was time for lunch! She jumped to her feet to be one of the first in the queue. In the dining hall, she got in line with her tray. Uncle Pierre, the cook, smiled at the girl whose big brown eyes sparkled with excitement. Pierre asked her if she was very hungry, hungry or not hungry. Malika thought carefully about the luscious and filling msemen she’d had for breakfast but eyed the colorful dishes prepared by the cook. “Very hungry,” she said confidently.

Uncle Pierre’s smile grew bigger. He turned to all the kids waiting behind Malika and announced, “The menu today is a Spring méli-mélo as a starter, a mushroom lasagna with Pierre’s ta-ra-ta-ta as a main and a strawberry panna cotta.” Pierre continued, “The bread is from Julia, whom you met last week when she came for the weekly breakfast, and the cheese is a delicious brousse from the municipal farm.”

Malika could barely wait for the end of the menu’s announcement. Behind Pierre, Sabrina and Fatima finished up sorting the small, medium and large plates. If a child said that he was not very hungry, they would give him a small plate. If he was hungrier, a larger one. At the end of the meal, the culinary team would weigh the total food waste. Teachers would then report to the children and gather feedback as to what had worked and what had not worked to minimize the waste. These conversations occurred during the weekly class “food, the environment and culture.” These were Malika’s favorite classes, even better than her science classes where she created her green water filter mechanism, harnessing natural plant processes to clean up a polluted water sample.

The meal was D-E-L-I-C-I-O-U-S, she had learned the new word in English and repeated it to her friends at the dining hall table. The Spring méli-mélo starter had revealed itself to be a medley of fresh bicolor radishes and zucchini tagliatelle with chickpeas marinated in a citrusy dressing. Pierre’s ta-ra-ta-ta was a favorite of Malika’s, a well-seasoned tofu ricotta that made the lasagna sheets melt in her mouth. She hadn’t liked the panna cotta as much because her gidda’s flan à la crème was incomparably superior but she devoured the fresh strawberries that topped the panna cotta. Malika had used the bread to chase the last few bits of mushroom in her ceramic plate and the brousse to add even more creaminess to the pasta. She remembered the soft fleece of the baby goats she had caressed in the municipal farm. The employees there had explained how they produced the milky, crumbly brousse and the other curated types of goat cheese that Malika also liked. She looked forward to the school breakfast next week. As part of the “food, the environment and culture” class, parents and teachers collaborated with one or more local producers to showcase a product and a personal story. Like many inhabitants of her neighborhood, Malika was the descendant of immigrants who had sought out better opportunities in France. Her neighbors were Algerian, like her family, but also Senegalese, Congolese, Armenian, Vietnamese. In the next weekly breakfast, they would make spring rolls, taught by Tanh, the mother of her best friend, Linh. An organic farmer from Alleins, about an hour’s drive away, would come with fresh cucumbers, carrots and aromatics to make the fragrant dish.

After lunch, Miss Lauret took them to the school garden. She taught children how to tend to the mint and the strawberries that were reddening under the warm sun of the afternoon. She did not try to stop children from plucking a few of the fruits. Happily, their supply came from local farmers who had a close partnership with the municipal department in charge of “food democracy,” not from the school’s humble garden whose main purpose was to have children learn and care about the living world that served to nourish them.

Malika watered the mint plot delicately, she loved the alluring scent of this herb. Her favorite dish was her gidda’s tikourvivine, semolina balls mixed with olive oil, eggs and mint, plunged into a rich red sauce filled with vegetables and a little bit of meat. Sometimes, her gidda left out the meat altogether and doubled down on mint and chickpeas. Malika loved how the semolina balls melted in her mouth. The mint, bits of green in the golden semolina and crimson sauce, looked like emeralds. Malika finished tending the plants and went on to class, where she sat to study history. Miss Lauret started, “Not too long ago, most people didn’t recognize that they were part of the living world, that without it, our planet was unlivable. They forgot that they had the responsibility to care for our world so that it would take care of ourselves in return. Last week, we learned about how people and governments made the brave decision to phase out entirely and forever, fossil fuels.” Malika listened attentively, she had watched movie clips of the massive protests and international conferences that had led to this revolution.

The teacher continued, “Today, we will learn how forty years ago, France and almost every other country in the world, shifted to a sustainable food system, respectful of the human and non-human that depend on each other to live beautiful lives…”

Malika left school at 4 p.m., holding her gidda’s wrinkled hand. “Gidda,” she said, “I can’t believe when you were young, people still exploited animals and put killers-of-life (Miss Lauret told them that then these products were euphemistically called insecticides and pesticides even if they killed everything and everyone) on the food they ate and on the soil that made it grow!”

Gidda coughed a little bit. “Yes, Malika, I remember that time. Most of us didn’t know what was going on. Those who knew did not want to change the system because they wanted to make money. Now it’s over. We have to repair the world we harmed. God willing, you children will know better than us and never repeat these same mistakes again.”

Malika and her gidda returned to their small apartment. That night, gidda fixed a simple meal, an egg shakshuka, which Malika ate with arlom, semolina bread made with olive oil and cooked on the stove. Gidda felt more tired than usual. When Malika’s mother, Lila, came back from work, she found her yemma, her mother almost asleep on the kitchen table. Her thin grayish hair sat loose on her frail shoulders. Yemma had left a portion of shakshuka and two carefully folded msemen for her daughter. She had meant to stay awake but a strange tiredness made her limbs feel like weights. Lila shook her yemma softly. “Ya yemma, ya yemma, you shouldn’t have stayed here. Go to sleep now; I will eat and come to sleep too.” Her mother looked up. Lila shivered, her yemma seemed to barely recognize her and appeared so tired. Lila felt scared and promised herself to take one or two days off to take her to the doctor. Lately, her yemma had been coughing a lot during her sleep. Lila and her mother shared one bedroom while Malika slept alone in the smaller one. Lila had wanted her daughter to have everything, a room of her own where she could study, rest and dream without worrying. Lila kept her eyes open during that night, she listened to the heavy breathing of her mother.

A few months later, gidda died. She had cancer, a consequence of working years during her adulthood as an immigrant farmer in Southern Europe where producers used killers-of-life. The European Union then subsidized industrial farming and the chemicals it used. Production and export imperatives mattered more than lives. The killers-of-life had taken their time but they had got gidda in the end.

The year of gidda’s death, Malika went on to middle school. There too, there was a garden where she would tend to plants. One day after lunch, she went to see the gardener, a kind-hearted woman in her late forties, and asked her if they could plant mint this year. Unlike her school garden, the middle school didn’t cultivate this aromatic, the gardener had limited space and wanted to test a few other plants like marigold, a surprising variety tasting of passion fruit and citrus. Looking carefully at Malika and seeing the sadness in her eyes, the gardener nodded. “Of course, I still have some seeds. You can come after your classes if you would like to plant them with me.” Malika gave her a grateful smile, tainted with sorrow, and came back later that afternoon. She planted the mint seeds silently, feeling a terrible ache in her chest. She prayed that the mint would grow strong and vibrant, like her gidda had been.

title: New Fires, Old Seeds
author: by Rue Sparks, United States of America

paragraphs: — 5 Years After The Burning —
Sparks licked the air above their campfire, cutting through the murky dusk. Each spark tasted the salt of rolling waves and tears on splotchy cheeks before melting into the soot of night.

Meredith cupped her hands around the infant fire, coaxing it to take hold. Too close, wispy red tattoos scorched her trembling fingers. She waited until the flames finished greedily devouring the twigs and sticks, then fed them the last rotting log.

She pulled Annalise close as the flames feasted; rubbed her daughters smaller hands between her own to share any residual warmth that lingered. Annalise leaned deep into her side, tangled brown curls tickling Meredith’s chin. Comfort was a luxury rarely afforded these days— moments when Annalise sought it even rarer. They’d had years to adjust to the absence of those baritone ramblings in her memory, but they’d not yet learned how to carry the same weight with two instead of three.

The crackle and snap of the fire gorging itself broke the quiet as the sun settled beneath the dunes. The once freshwater lakes had become briny and rancid, the water line retreating more and more every year.
With the slow contamination and climbing temperatures, the land itself dried and withered.

It was like the world had shed its carapace too early, revealing a malformed, underdeveloped larvae underneath that mummified in the open air. Even the wind was too humbled to sing through the endless brackish water that was once Lake Huron.
“I thought it would be smaller,” Annalise said, the first words to break the landscape in what must have been months.
The oily lake bed sprawled ahead of them, observing them through its death rattle.
— 8 Years Before The Burning —
“Do we lose something for everything gained?” Daniel whispered, his cold cheek meeting Meredith’s.

This night had brimmed with life, the song of crickets and cicadas a lullaby that had coaxed Annalise to slumber. Through the slit of their tent, Meredith watched their toddler’s fingers curl into her sleeping bag, arm around her ratty stuffed tiger.
“What could we possibly have traded for her?” she whispered. Their noses bumped together as they clung to the warmth of their breath and words.

Daniel grabbed another log, arranging it carefully on the remaining embers. The flames tested its bark, debating whether the sacrifice it’d been offered was worth its blessing. Daniel had been quiet for a while, but Meredith recognized the lips stretched over clenched teeth, muscles tight, chewing on his thoughts. Both Daniel and Annalise were like that, ruminating on the mysteries of the universe and kindergarten in the hushed in-betweens.
The fire tore into the sacrifice before Daniel tucked his reply into her neck. “I don’t think the universe is a zero sum game. Things happen. We gain some things, we lose some things.”
It sounded so simple then. The vagaries of the universe laid out between them. The symphony of nocturnal insects and private murmurs replaced with silence.
“The value of everything we lose and gain is up to each of us,” he’d said, the chorus of cicadas threatening to overcome his voice in the night.
“Oxygen is to a tree what carbon dioxide is to us.”
— 6 Years After The Burning —

“We’re going to see the tree, right?” Annalise asked. It was now a few hours since they’d passed the husk of Alpena. They traveled along the jagged edges of what was left of the shoreline. The black sludge of decaying seaweed and dead fish that floated atop the shallow water painted their rubber waders dark, even in the waning sun.

Meredith tried to gather an answer in her mind, but the putrid sloshing of their boots and the rancid and salty air stifled her concentration. The horizon felt sharp on her eyes and her memory, the edges threatening to cut her.
“We’re going to the cabin,” she settled on carefully. “Not the tree. If either of them are even there.”
“It’s there,” Annalise said, between chattering teeth. “The tree. I just know it.”

When the cold became unbearable, Meredith lit a fire with their last proper log, resigned to finding more fuel and supplies in the morning. Annalise had gone through what would probably be her last growth spurt—yet shorter than she would have been had she been a teen with adequate nutrition. But regardless, her faded and ripped jeans came up to her ankles, shirt stretched thin beyond simple wear.

Meredith had herself lived hand to mouth as a child. She never wanted that for her daughter, but the world had other plans. Her mind pulled her to keep them marching North, but the threat of cold and starvation would win if she did. It always did in the end.

She wondered not for the first time if they should be searching out a larger group. It’d been months since they’d seen a soul, and even then Meredith had pulled Annalise back to hide amongst the ruins of a rusted and collapsing warehouse until they’d passed.
Desperate people stop acting like people, she’d told herself. The cabin has supplies, it’s remote, it’s defensible. We can only trust us two now.

She poked a dried sprig of dune grass into the flames, and the fire took it, hot air rising off the flames twirled the grass into a mournful ballet until all that remained were glimpses of sparks. They floated like a constellation before fading, the night returning to its black cage of clouds above them.
It was a relief, this pitch-black night. The starless cosmos felt far more comforting than the night the sky had burned.
— 6 Years Before The Burning —
Across another fire, Daniel watched a patchwork of stars between rolling clouds.
“Did you know there are pine cones that only open with fire?”
He twisted part of a pine cone between his fingers, tracing the edges like he was trying to memorize it.

Another era, another campfire. Annalise in the tent, its canopy bright and unblemished. They’d finally given in to her begging for a new one, her old tent becoming too small for her growing legs. It was colder, far later in the fall than they normally camped. But there had been rumblings, an anxious murmur no one yet wished to acknowledge. When Daniel had suggested one last trip before the snow hit, Meredith had seen the edge of fear in his eyes.

“Seems like a weird evolutionary trait,” Meredith said. Daniel’s existential meanderings had once entranced her. Now, they dug into fresh wounds. “How often would there need to be fires for that to work?”

“Wildfires didn’t used to be what they are now,” he’d said. There was a spark in his words again, an afterimage under eyelids of the before. “Nowadays every year the whole of California’s burning, but we’ve made it that way. Or at least allowed it.”
Meredith knew it was her turn to talk. This pattern, this dance they’d fostered over the years demanded it. Theirs was a love of curiosity and questions. Reciprocity of wonder.
It felt obligatory, now. A role she no longer wanted, or couldn’t fill.
The silence stretched, and the little excitement Daniel regained bled from him. He melted into the back of the chair, continuing to speak, but lacking his typical awe.

“Indigenous tribes like the Karuk and Yoruk had this practice of cultural burning. They would burn areas of land to promote biodiversity, minimize endemics of parasitic insects. Basically prevent wildfires from wreaking havoc.” He flung the pine cone into the flames. The fire released a few halfhearted pops as the seeds caught, then fell quiet.

“Any of those pine cones around here?” Meredith asked. They’d been seeing less and less acorns and pine cones. She couldn’t remember the last time she’d seen any of the plants in their travels survive long enough to produce seeds.
“The ones I’m thinking of were on the West Coast,” Daniel said. He shrugged, a flinch that was near unrecognizable burrowed into the ratty camping chair. “But I suppose it’s possible.”

“Well, if everything burns, at least maybe trees will take our place,” Meredith said. She remembered being a child, scraped hands and torn jeans from climbing trees. Getting caught in brambles and picking wild raspberries, hands stained red from the juice.
Annalise knew so little of that world. She knew more of salt and sand than wild raspberries and petrichor.
“They were here before us. It’s nice, actually. To think they might survive us,“ Daniel said.
It had been one more thing they'd disagreed on.
— 7 Years After The Burning —

The Soo Locks seemed so much smaller now. Once a marvel of human ingenuity, the concrete crumbled into the poisoned lakewater. Trails of rust seeped from untended machinery, the locks unreliable from years of disuse. They camped on the Michigan side of the bridge, the sun peeking between the railings as it descended toward the horizon.
“It’s kinda weird,” Annalise said. “So many things got destroyed or crumbled. But the sunset is still pretty.”

It was a bit early for a campfire, but they’d made it to Saul Ste Marie earlier than planned. Annalise’s feet were blistered, soles of shoes worn to thin strips. Meredith’s were blistered too, deeply cracked and peeling. They’d been crushed into the too-small hiking boots they’d found in an abandoned Dollar General.

“Your father would’ve said something about beauty existing even in the most dire circumstances. He saw things in ways others didn’t.” Meredith mouth had spoken the word before she registered the thought. His absence felt like a faraway memory some days, the sharp edges soothed with time.
Yet remembering him out loud felt like a different hurt.

She forced herself to her feet, unsteady at first as the horizon swayed in her sight. They needed to find more food. Their early arrival to the remains of the city opened up the possibility of combing through what buildings remained.

“What about me? You used to say I’m like him.” Annalise said. She watched Meredith dig into their packs, contemplating what they should ditch to save room and weight. It hurt Meredith to look at those familiar green eyes full of curiosity, now on a more rounded, youthful face.
She felt imbalanced again, but this time it had nothing to do with starvation.
“You’re my daughter too. There’s as much of me in you as him.”
— 6 Years Before The Burning —

The fire burned hot and wild, but the warmth didn’t reach either of them. The cold space between them felt like miles. Meredith wondered how they’d managed to travel so far apart while sharing the same oxygen.
“Do you think the first human to burn a tree for warmth knew where that path would take us? Not warming hands, but the planet we live on?” Daniel had asked, unable to bear the weight of silence.
But the words seemed rote, edges dull and fettered by exhaustion.

“Not now. I’m tired. There’s too much to think about.” Meredith could still peek at Annalise through the tent flap, the once shiny and new fabric dulled and stained. Even at a distance she could smell the underlying mustiness that they could never quite get out of the fabric.
“We need to restock,” Meredith began. “Annalise has been wearing the same two sweaters for months.
They’re worn to threads. She hasn’t complained, but I see her shivering, even though she—”

“There’s nothing we can do about it right this second,” Daniel said. His tone forced her to face him, his eyes not the vibrant green she used to lose herself in. The color seemed sickly, murky. And behind that, steel. Meredith was struck by how many wrinkles lined his eyes now. How few of them were likely from laughter and joy.
“Let’s just pretend,” he pleaded. “Just for tonight. That things are what they were back then. Before the dawn breaks and everything is unavoidable in the light of day.”
He was right, about this at least. If nothing else, Annalise deserved her rest.

“Fine,” she bit out. She searched her memory for the thread of Daniel’s current rambling. “I doubt they knew what it would mean. How could they.”’ Daniel shook his head, ever the contrarian. “By the time humans were able to use fire as a tool they should have had the cognitive ability to—“ “They were cold, Daniel,” Meredith said firmly. Like she’d borrowed steel from his eyes and built her own stronghold from it. “When push comes to shove, we do what we have to. Maybe one day we can debate philosophy again, but our bodies need more than academic debate and existential thought experiments to survive.”
It’d been quiet for many months now. No matter where they wandered, no matter which direction or how far, the silence dogged their steps. The Earth itself seemed to be quieting as the years passed.
The quiet had never felt quite so scorching until that moment.
“I know,” Daniel whispered. He stared at the fire, his limbs still. Like something in him had been snuffed out.
“Does it even matter? If they’d known?” she said eventually. She wasn’t sure if she wished to coax him back into himself, back to her side, or if she wanted to hurry the inevitable break.
“Ask the forests.”
— 7 Years After The Burning —

In the Upper Peninsula, scattered copses of trees gave way to a mimicry of forest. Along the edges the decay was newer, ground piled with recently dead or fallen trees. The bite of damp leaves in the air became nearly unbearable as they maneuvered their way deeper into the trees.

The once packed soil and gravel of the trail toward the cabin was interrupted by fallen trees and mass erosion. They maneuvered around a particularly large section of decay, stone and brittle foliage that seemed to have been swept into this flat part of the forest during a flash flood.
It left the area unrecognizable. By the time Meredith looked up from watching her footholds, she didn’t understand what she saw.
The cabin was in ruins.
— 6 Years After The Burning —

‘We didn’t know. What it would all lead to, those first fires of desperate men. We never do.’ Daniel’s sprawling handwriting curled and blackened as the page burned. Daniel’s notebook, lined pages worn and water stained. One of many epistolary ramblings he’d left scattered across their lives like breadcrumbs.
They’d run out of kindling. The shoreline had become dry and desolate, all salt-covered rock and cracked soil. They’d burned what little paper ephemera they had on them. The worst of their clothing.
Anything they could afford to sacrifice to flame.
The notebook was the last.
They knitted their limbs together, hovered over the flames. Warmed the worst of themselves, trembling fingers and frozen feet.
“We’re going to make it,” Annalise said, words and breath so close. If Meredith closed her eyes, she might be convinced they were her own. “We have to.”
There was one page left. No more photos. No more notes. No more proof of Daniel’s existence to carry, even though sometimes she thought she hated him more than she ever loved him.

‘We never know which thing we destroy will become a wall in front of us, or which thing we build will destroy us.’ The words crimped into themselves, black consuming the page before it too became ash.
— The Burning —
Like most terrible things, it started out beautiful.

They’d been at the cabin for several weeks by then, taking periodic trips to scour nearby towns and trade with anyone they came across. The building was solid, built to withstand storms and blistery winters. Their stories grew from what they could carry with them, the advent of a familiar basecamp doing much to soothe Meredith’s anxiety and Annalie’s fear.
Then the storm hit.
Lightning arced across the sky, blinding despite the cloak the falling snow had lain over the atmosphere. It spanned the horizon in spiderweb cracks that reached beyond the hills.
There was a hot, toxic smell in the air.

“I wanna see,” Annalise said. Meredith clenched the puffy fabric of Annalise’s coat tight enough to cramp her fingers. Their daughter may now be old enough to contemplate the mysteries of the universe, but she was young enough to still believe in her own invincibility.
“It’s not safe,” Meredith said. The preteen tried to pull away, to leave the safety of the cabin’s porch.
“But Dad’s out there,” she whispered, and Meredith could hear the tinge of worry this time. Not misplaced bravery. Fear.
“Dad’s being an idiot,” Meredith said, squeezing tighter.

“Daniel, get back inside!” she yelled into the night. When he’d first walked out, he’d been a murky silhouette in the falling snow, but it was slowing. He was wrapping a chain around a tree near the shore, connected to the two skiffs they used for the creek. The storm had come on so suddenly they’d been unable to store them.
A flash, and lightning illuminated the sky. Thunder cracked only a second afterward.
“It’s not the first time we’ve seen thunder snow.” He grabbed the chain around the tree, wiggled it to test its security. “I’m just going to—”

“I don’t like this, Dan,” she interrupted. Annalise had stopped trying to break from her hold, but there was static, a current in the air. Daniel had taken a couple steps back toward the cabin when his short- cropped hair stood on end.
“All good. Let’s get inside, we—“ The crack of lightning swallowed her sense.
Light and heat scorched through the black—the brightest day chiseled itself into the night for a blink.
Her eyes burned in its wake.
She stared up at a sky brimming with stars and crackles of lightning through thin clouds, but couldn’t remember falling.
A hand in hers—smaller, cold, Annalise. Screaming, but her head felt constricted, a constant pitch in her ears stealing the sound. Smoke in her lungs, fire eating through brambles and trees.

She looked for him, but saw only the tree. It now bore a long, jagged scar up its trunk. Flames engulfed the interior, bark and branches somehow escaping the flames. Behind it, the brackish water of the creek still sizzled, aftershocks of lightning jumping between the metal boats and the water’s surface.
The crackle of thunder would rumble in her bones for many hours later, burned into the marrow. Like fire contained in the husk of a tree.
Daniel was on the ground.
— 7 Years After The Burning —
“What’s the likelihood of the same place being struck by lightning twice?” Meredith asked. There was no answer.

The silence wasn’t surprising. Annalise had been quiet since they’d arrived. After the immediate shock faded, they’d started digging through the remains of the cabin. Silent, thorough. Searching for anything intact, anything useful. Annalise avoided Meredith’s gaze, picking through the rubble with the same listless movements that plagued Daniel in his worst depressions.

The years had worn through expectations and hope until all that remained was resignation and a stubborn doggedness to just keep moving. Now they’d returned to where they’d lost that last fragment of hope along with Daniel. All these years they’d run from the empty void that had made it’s home in this forest only to find the pit dug deeper.
They worked into the evening, the air of futility growing thicker as the sky darkened. Eventually Annalise stopped altogether, staring toward the creek with deadened eyes.
Meredith touched her shoulder cautiously. “Hey. We’ll figure something out.”
Annalise shook her head. Now standing beside her, Meredith realized it wasn’t the creek Annalise was looking at it.
The tree was still there.

The fire had long since burned itself out, but the tree remained. The branches on one side had died, much of them falling when they became too dry and brittle. The other side was alive but hadn’t grown, the lack of nutrients in the soil or groundwater leaving it in stasis.
Except for a few delicate buds clinging to life on a single branch, reaching toward the creek. One last impossibility as the world burned.

They walked towards it, their footfalls the only sound. Annalise raised a shaking hand to the edges of the lightning’s scar, tracing the edge to its lowest point. She reached inside until her entire forearm was swallowed by it.
When she pulled it back, in her hand she held a pine cone. It was half gone, only a few scales remaining intact.
“Some pine cones only open with fire,” Annalise whispered. She held her hand between them, the cone nestled into the heart of her palm. A broken and halved thing.
She met Annalise’s eyes. Daniel’s eyes. An endless green that might survive past the forests they mirrored. No longer a child or preteen, but an adult. A young woman grown into her own strength.
“I think we’ve had enough fires, don’t you?”

Long, long ago, before Brother Moon chased Sister Sun into the deepness of the sky, back when we were all alone in the world, Nuliajuk lived with her parents and their sled dogs. She had long, thick hair and a favourite dog with fur of red and white. Her ataata Anguta wanted her to get married, but she spurned all of the men who came to visit. None of them moved so lightly across the ice as did her dog. None were as brave or quick or strong, and Nuliajuk doubted any man could love her even half as much.

Each time Nuliajuk awoke, Anguta and her anaana Isarrataitsoq asked her why she hadn’t yet chosen any of the men who came calling. They were good, strong men, and an additional hunter would help keep starvation at bay. Food was so hard to find in the days before seals, fish, whales, and walruses. Nuliajuk was annoyed with this. As she combed her hair she said her truth: “None of them will make as good a husband as the red and white dog.”

This made her ataata angry, and when she proudly gestured to her taut bulging belly, the fire of his rage flared higher. He was so repulsed, he decided he would be rid of her for once and for all. That would be one less mouth to feed.
Anguta forced Nuliajuk into his qajaq. He paddled out to the small island of Pitektaryuk.

He abandoned his daughter there and paddled home. When he got back to the camp, his wife Isarrataitsoq had filled packs with food and tools. She glared at Anguta while strapping them to her daughter’s dog-husband.

Nuliajuk had been right. Her dog-husband was loyal, brave, and strong. Certainly more loyal and brave than her ataata. The red and white dog jumped into the freezing water and quickly swam all the way out to Pitektaryuk to take care of his bride. She dried him off with eider down and they snuggled together to keep warm.

Every day, the dog carried packs of food from Nuliajuk’s parents to his wife. With his assistance, Nuliajuk had made a hut to shelter herself from the elements. Her qulliq kept her warm while he was away. Then came the day when she birthed their litter. Some of their children took after her and were humans. Some took after their ataata and were dogs. And some took after both and were born as polar bears: those who make one frightened.

Isarrataitsoq rebuked Anguta for exiling their daughter. For leaving her to give birth all alone with only a dog to care for her. Anguta threw up his hands and told his wife he’d do better. He loaded the dog’s pack himself. But as he thought about how Nuliajuq had chosen to marry a dog instead of one of the young men who had come calling, a high tide of rage rose in his heart. He put stones in the pack and hid them with a thin layer of meat on top so Isarrataitsoq could not see what he had done.

When the red and white dog stepped into the water, the heavy pack pulled him to the deep dark of the sea. Anguta’s conscience spoke too loudly for him to ignore, and he took meat to Nuliajuk, himself.

Nuliajuk waited and waited for her dog-husband to return to her, and when she instead saw her ataata’s qajaq, she knew what must have happened. Nuliajuk and her children were outraged. Mad with hunger and grief, Nuliajuk devoured one of his arms. The dogs and the polar bears chased their ataata back to his qajaq, and he paddled away back home as fast as he could with just one arm.

Now Nuliajuk didn’t have enough to feed her children or herself. She nursed her babies until her breasts went dry, and then she sang lullabies. She put her human children into one of her kamiit, gave them three straws to use as masts, and they drifted east across the ocean to become the ancestors of white people. Her puppies she put into the outer sole of her boot, and they drifted across the land to become the ancestors of the Chipewyan. Her polar bear cubs left and became the ever-wandering ones. She stayed by herself on Pitektaryuk until her maimed ataata returned again out of shame, and this time he brought his young widowed daughter back home.
Nuliajuk missed her children. She mourned her missing dog-husband. Staying at the camp with the murderer of the red and white dog only reminded her of what had been taken away.

One day, while Anguta was out hunting, she saw a strange qajaq in the distance. It was paddled by a big man wearing snow goggles. Eager to get away, she waved him ashore. This, she decided, would be her new husband. She packed her qulliq, her ulu, and her sewing needles, got into the qajaq with him, and they paddled off to his home. She was glad to see the last of her ataata’s hunting camp. Good riddance, she thought.

Her new husband’s paddle dipped like wings into the ocean. The qajaq flew between ice floes across the surface of the sea. Nuliajuk was surprised at how light he was on the water considering how big a man he was.

At last they arrived at her new home on a distant island, and when he got out, Nuliajuk realised he only looked big because he’d perched atop a high seat in the qajaq. His legs were very short. And then he took off his goggles and revealed hideous red, lidless eyes. She stared at his strange face and long beak with its tube-shaped nostrils. He stripped off his parka and stretched out his wings.

He was not a man at all! He was a fulmar disguised as one. Nuliajuk wept at how she’d been tricked by this shapechanger. To make matters even worse, her new husband was a terrible hunter and shit everywhere. He brought home very little to eat and the skins he brought back were too small and too filled with holes to be useful. Though she worked hard to make their tent habitable, the wind blew through the tears and chilled her to the bone. Her qulliq was not enough to keep her warm, and the birds on the island attacked her whenever she got too close to their eggs.

Nuliajuk cried and cried. She sat on a shit-speckled rock by the shore and stared off toward her old home longingly. Living with her parents was far better than where she was now, cold, hungry, and surrounded by bird poop. Oh how she missed that hunting camp now.
Living with a dog-murderer was better than living with this bird. Living with the constant nagging that she take a human husband was not nearly as bad as being on this desolate island.
At least back at the camp she’d had someone to talk to. At least her family didn’t shit where they slept. At least there she had been warm and had meat to eat.

All this time, Isarrataitsoq missed her daughter terribly. She sent Anguta out to find Nuliajuk, telling him not to return without her. Every day, Anguta slowly paddled around in his qajaq, searching every island, iceberg, and ice floe until he saw her waving from a faraway rocky shore. She looked so thin. She looked so forlorn. He felt bad that she was living so poorly, and so did she. And so she got into the qajaq with him one last time and they floated away.

While they were still out in the open water, Nuliajuk’s fulmar husband flew home and could not find his wife. This infuriated him, and he flew around with a flock of other birds until he found her with her ataata. Anguta paddled faster to get away, but the bird husband and the flock flapped their wings so hard that a great storm arose. The waves were high and treacherous. The wind and the chop threatened to flip Anguta and Nuliajuk into the icy water.

The screeching birds kept right on flapping and flapping, and in terror that the qajaq would flood and be sunk, Anguta ordered Nuliajuk to get out. She refused, of course, and they began to fight, which only threatened all the more to sink their boat which sat very low in the water.

Anguta bashed his daughter across the head with his paddle. Half stunned, she fought back, but he held a paddle and she did not. He hit her again and again with it until she was knocked out into the slushy water. Nuliajuk grabbed the gunwales and tried to pull herself back in, but Anguta would not allow it. Instead, he smashed her hands over and over again with the paddle, shattering her hands until little pieces of her fingers and thumbs pattered like hailstones into the sea.
No longer able to clutch, the bleeding Nuliajuk sank beneath the surface into the abyss.

When the fulmar saw that his wife was gone beneath the waves, the birds let the storm calm and they flew back to their island. The bird husband circled around a few more times, gazing down at the water. It was pink from her blood, as bright as the throats of his hungry chicks.
He could not join her underwater, so he flew away as well. Now that the water was calm, Anguta paddled his way home, abandoning Nuliajuk for the last time.

Deep in the Arctic Ocean, Nuliajuk’s finger and thumb joints shook and grew, transforming into the anirniliit, all the breathing creatures of the sea. From her phalanges emerged whales and walruses and seals. The blood from her smashed hands transformed into all the fishes: cod, char, sculpins and more. She sank further and further until she got to Adlivun, the land at the bottom of the sea, and then her children gave her a tail like that of a fish. She screamed, flailed her arms, and shook her head and tail until the water boiled up in another storm. It sent a huge wave to wash over her parents’ hunting camp, dragging Isarrataitsoq and Anguta down into Adlivun with her. Now this was their home, too.

Far below the surface, Nuliajuk’s thick, strong hair flowed around her like tangled strands of kelp. Though she was filled with rage at her betrayal, she was no longer alone. The seals, the fishes, the walruses, the whales, visited her far beneath the ice. They always came when she called them. They snuggled up to her in the knots of her hair to keep her warm. From the tangles of her tresses they sang her songs and kept her company.

Though the bird storm was gone and the storm of Nuliajuk’s anger had calmed, the people of the surface world grew hungrier. They split their camps up and wandered the land looking for things to eat, but there wasn’t enough to feed them. But when they were nearer to the water, there were all sorts of things to eat if they were respectful. The children of Nuliajuk took pity on their human cousins. The anirniliit offered themselves to the people to eat.

Nuliajuk demanded the humans respect her children born of her blood and phalanges. She demanded that the humans give the gift of fresh water to the anirniliit, placing it within the mouths of those who offered themselves up in order that humans might survive. If the humans killed more than they needed, if they took too long to kill, if they killed out of bloodlust, or if they only wounded the anirniliit and let them suffer, well, then Nuliajuk called her children back to her and let the humans starve to death.

Sometimes these hungry people might glimpse a seal, a whale, a walrus, or a fish in the distance. But try as they might, no one could catch one. And this is why when there is nothing to eat, an angakkuq must take on the form of a nanook, one of Nuliajuk’s polar bear children. And then they must swim down to the bottom of the sea to placate Nuliajuk by combing her thick and tangled hair. Without fingers, she cannot do it herself. When her anger is assuaged and the angakkuq promises the anirniliit will be respected, some of her children swim away from their anaana and once again offer themselves up to us to eat.

Nuliajuk is still down there at the bottom of the sea. She lives in a house with a whalebone frame and with the walls made from the clothing of all who drown. She and her family oversee the spirits of wicked and lazy people, teaching them so that they may be reborn anew and do better in their next lives. Nuliajuk’s red and white dog guards their camp at the bottom of the sea while her hair sways back and forth in the current like kelp.
She has her eye on those who poison the ocean and melt its ice. They are not changing their ways. She plans another starving time.

Wild-haired woman of the water, Forced and flung from Anguta’s qajaq, Mother to the sea with ice floes for clouds, His paddle smashes finger phalanges.
Forced and flung from Anguta’s qajaq, Bleeding broken fingers transform His paddle smashes finger phalanges.
Anirniliit with flippers and fins.
Bleeding broken fingers transform And a phalanx becomes a whale Anirniliit with flippers and fins Nuliajuk will never again be alone.

And a phalanx becomes a whale.
Her phantom fingers breathe and swim.
Nuliajuk will never again be alone.
She makes their camp in Adlivun.

Her phantom fingers breathe and swim.
Drip sweet water from your mouth to theirs.
She makes their camp in Adlivun.
We must maintain equilibrium.

Drip sweet water from your mouth to theirs.
I speak to you of Nuliajuk.
We must maintain equilibrium.

I speak to you of Nuliajuk,
Wild-haired woman of the water,

Mother to the sea with ice floes for clouds.

It’s dark in the silo. Space dark like a million light years from the sun. Grave dark like death itself or an absence of light, life. Still. Silent. Strangely seductive. Almost morbid in its absence. Still. The Pro Ks don’t care. Their nucleus absent existence doesn’t subject them to fear. Dark, light, inner, outer, life, death. It’s one and the same. An endless process. A changing. A transformation. A reformation. It is not alive. More a living thing. Almost like a thought process. A fear. An irrational phobia. Like humans fear germs. Microscopic organisms that in the wrong place at the wrong time can be fatal. Escherichia-coli attacking the kidneys. Meningitis disrupting the neuronal pathways. Streptococcus invading the red rivers of life.

But, like an endless painting by MC Escher, the Pro Ks progress. They never give up. Never relent. Because relenting is an action. They are active yet passive. They are neutral but charged with energy. They are all pervading. Ever multiplying. Ever progressing. Ever digesting. Ever corrupting. Ever decomposing. Ever degenerating. Just like us.

It was the similarities between bacteria and human behaviour that first caught the attention of newly graduated microbiologist Kathe Kovak. Six months out of Bristol University School of Science and Technology and now stationed at the former Drax Power Station in North Yorkshire. Trading clinical test tube efficiency for post industrial desolation. A blot on the landscape. A sore on the sublime. A scab that returned to work during strike. Because that’s what capitalism demanded. Shrinking rights. Increasing profits. Deadening determination with the cold blow of threat. Coal burned at 20 million tonnes of CO2 a year. That’s a threat!
Now lying dormant. Left to rot. Still to pollute. Still a blight. But how to reverse that process?
Reclaim the human damage to the natural environment. Revive the energy of that nightmare place.
It was during a late-night experiment in the labs of BSST that the idea first came to her.

Humans. What were they but parasites on the land. Destroyers of the landscape. A plague on the planet. She looked through the microscopic lens at the beautifully repellant bacteria on the petri dish and saw herself reflected in the mindless movements of the bacteria. Not herself as an individual. But herself as a movement. Like some vague Marxist notion of mob existence. Humans acting en masse with symbiotic certainty. Sure to cause pain and suffering. Violence and vilification. As the brainless genomes multiplied before her eyes, she saw the subtle symmetry like a brutal beating. Humans shagging. Brainlessly aimlessly reproducing. Populating the planet with generations of polluters. Barking forth fumes and farts. Methane and CO2. Always consuming and destroying. Pretending to care. Empty government targets. Vacant carbon neutral pledges. Always focused on profits. Shares and dividends. Second homes and secret salaries. While Greece burned and India drowned.
Cornwall crumbled and the Maldives became the new Atlantis.

And she saw it so clearly. Like a religious revelation. An alcoholic’s moment of clarity. The solution. And it was not in a mandate or a speech to a nation. It was not conducted in the corridors of power or thought up over roast quail at a private members club in Westminster.

It was there. In her mind. In the lens before her eyes. In the way all ideas have always been there. Just waiting to be found. Waiting to evolve. To reach the next stage. The latest transcendence. The new saviour for our times.
At first, she’d struggled at Drax. The neanderthal engineering mindset. The politics of cost.

The reluctance towards innovation. But when she’d shown them the results. The endless power of the Pro Ks. Their insatiable appetite for consuming. Like us, she’d said. Can you see the parallels? she’d asked. Nodding heads like non-nucleic entities themselves. Yes. How brilliant Kathe. How wonderful. Wow. You’re going to be the 21st century’s answer to… And the praise went on against a backdrop of formulaic decay.
The Pro Ks’ progress was like a carbon eating pandemic. Like Covid on hyperdrive. The plague on amphetamines. They captured the CO2. Converted nitrogen to ammonia.

Changing the nitrates to plant fodder. Then when the autotrophs combined with the heterotrophs and blended with the chemotrophs. It was like nothing they’d ever witnessed before. It was nature at its most efficient. It was humanity’s individual insight played out on the world stage. It was instant evolution before their eyes. It was a chemical combination. A minor biological divergence. A circular existence. A contained cycle of self-containment.
Self-consumption. Eating decay. Embracing every compound in their thoughtless embrace.
Metallic, organic, rock, plastic polymer. All consumed by their effortless appetite. So simple.
So obvious. But so overlooked and unlikely that it had taken an existential catastrophe to stimulate a response.

After a year of Drax experimentation, Kathe Kovak perfected the formula. The Pro Ks worked so quickly. They eroded pollution. They dined on decay. They were adamant of their existence. Though delightfully ignorant of the role they played. They had no personal preference. They had been engineered to succeed. Spliced for success. Planned to perfection. Soon the nights turned to days. The darkness became. The endless silo nights were set to work. They were left to their own devices. It was a triumph.
The Pro K plan was rolled out across Europe. In the slate mines of Spain. In the coal fields of Poland. In the former gas works of Norway. In the fracked furrows of Hungary and Bulgaria.

Blights on the fjords. A cancer on the savanna. A dirt black stain on the fortresses of democracy. Now they were in remission. The world was in remission. The sea levels fell for the third year running. Lower temperatures were recorded year on year. New ice formed in the Arctic Sea. CO2 emissions halved. New species of plants and insects emerged. Humanity breathed a collective sigh of relief. Their time had been extended. Their injury time was now indefinite. Three cheers to the Pro Ks.

But Kathe Kovak sat and wondered. Stared at her laptop screen. Vacant eyes. Unresolved questions. Metaphysical ponderings. Now an advisor on climate change politics. Ted talks bringing in six figure sums. From her home on the Northumberland coast. Lindisfarne on the horizon. Promises of prayer and salvation. From some unknown force. Some invisible sin.

She sat at her laptop, but she stared at her window. A framed photo of her success. A blind mirror to the natural world. The brutal beauty of the North Sea. Lapping and thrashing mindlessly. Moon bent madness bringing equilibrium to life. Jet washed shores of tidal trembling. Cod rich depths. Oil free platforms. But something bothered her. For all the success of the Pro K project. The plaudits. The prizes. The fortune. The pseudo fame. Her name in the annals of achievement. An inspiration for the next generation. For all this, she was not content. There was something empty about it. Something lacking in her accomplishments. Something hollow in her philosophy. Humanity still produced. Still fought wars over indistinct borders. Still maimed and slaughtered over ancient ideologies. Still grasped and groped for glory. Still raped and plundered the land that she so longed to preserve.

Pro K had worked. It had reversed climate change. It had found a way to counteract the destruction of industry. Those microscopic prokaryote anomalies. Those single cell systemic saviours. Her anomalies. Her saviours. So why wasn’t she happy? Why wasn’t she content?

What more did she want than more than most people ever dream possible? Then, suddenly she saw it all. From her laptop near the window. With the North Sea in full swell. Heaving with planetary power. Like a child first sees their parents and understands that they are not ineffable. The realization that you are not immortal. Or are you? The awareness of your illogical existence. That was it. She had saved the world. Well, the Pro Ks had saved the world. But they hadn’t changed the attitude. Of all the people she’d met. The great scientific minds of the day. The most erudite intellectual thinkers of our time. The most compassionate humanitarians ever to exist. There was still a lack. And again, it was in the Pro Ks that she saw it.

The mindless organisms. The saviours of humanity. They had acted as a single cell organism as they had acted as a multiplying infinity of non-nucleic entities. Their aimless goal had been the same. Their urge. Their non-desire. Their organic destiny had not changed as it had multiplied. It had grown. It had become more than its single self. But it had not changed its action or its result.

That was it. She knew now. Kathe Kovak saw the aim of humanity. She saw it in the Pro Ks’ behaviour. She saw it in the tidal sway. She saw it in the starling’s murmuration. In the mushroom carpeting of the forest floor. In the canopies formation at the forest’s heights. It was collective action. Humans individual versus humans combined. How powerful and insightful we could be if we combined our consciousness. How we could progress our ideas and world view if only we could share our minds. We could move as one. We could embrace the cool transcendence of our spirits. Our place in the universe. We could unite science and spirituality. Do away with restrictive and cruel religious bias. Create a world in the image of the first visionaries based on the insights of a species without thought or goal.
Kathe Kovak shut down her laptop. She closed her eyes. She embraced the black night of her thoughts. Crystals of infinite wonder. A microbiocracy of perpetual peace. And she laughed.

A deep maniacal laugh. A sardonic laugh at the idiocy of it all. The satire of science. Saved by microbes. The amoeba becomes. The head of the food chain. As it always was. As it always will be. Saved for today. Gone tomorrow. Thank you, Pro Ks, for another chance at glory!

Fifty years later and the world no longer looked wounded. Not outwardly. The old scars had faded beneath blankets of green abundance. Former motorways cracked under the pressure of roots and rainwater. Shopping centres became limestone caverns for bats and nesting birds. Tankers rusted silently in ports reclaimed by salt marsh and reeds. Humanity called it recovery. Redemption. Renewal. Nature called it digestion.
The Pro Ks never stopped.

That was the first mistake. Humanity had believed in completion. In endings. We think in narratives because narratives comfort us. Beginning. Middle. End. But the Pro Ks did not recognise conclusion. They consumed because consumption was their nature. Their purpose absent purpose. Their endless becoming.

At first the changes were celebrated. Landfills vanished. Oceans cleared. Air became alpine crisp even in the old industrial capitals. Asthma rates collapsed. Cancer fell. Crops flourished in exhausted soils. The atmosphere stabilised. Children born in Beijing and Delhi could see stars again. Actual stars. Not satellites pretending to be heavens.
Then came the disappearances.
Plastic first. Synthetic fabrics next. Concrete weakening in strange geometric fractures.
Bridges dissolving slowly at the molecular level. Carbon composites turning brittle. Medical implants failing inside human bodies. Pacemakers eroding. Artificial hips flaking into powder.
The Pro Ks had evolved. Or perhaps they had merely continued. Humanity was the one that failed to keep pace.

Kathe Kovak had died twenty years earlier. State funeral. Memorial forests planted in her honour. Her speeches replayed in schools and government chambers. Saint Kathe. Saviour of Earth. The woman who gave humanity another century.
But in hidden forums and encrypted archives, another version survived. Grainy interviews.
Forgotten essays. Nervous warnings buried beneath celebration. She had known. Not fully.

But enough. The final years of her life had become increasingly isolated. Increasingly strange. She spoke less about climate and more about surrender. About collective consciousness. About relinquishing ownership of the planet itself.
Most dismissed her as brilliant but broken. The burden of genius. The rot of age.
Yet her final unpublished journal remained.
The last entry was only three lines long.
The Pro Ks are not correcting the planet for us.
They are correcting it from us.
And perhaps that is the same thing.

Now the cities dimmed earlier each year. Not from policy but from collapse. Steel support beams foamed into reddish dust beneath towers. Datacentres overheated as cooling systems failed. Satellites dropped from orbit because replacement materials degraded too quickly to sustain infrastructure. Humanity adapted where it could. Smaller communities.
Organic materials. Living architecture grown from fungal composites and engineered coral structures that the Pro Ks ignored. For now.
And still the microorganisms spread.
Silent. Tireless. Beautiful in their indifference.
Children born into this new world no longer feared them. They were taught coexistence from infancy. Never build too much. Never take too much. Never assume permanence.

Entire religions emerged around microbial balance. New monks cultivated bacterial gardens in underground chambers once used as missile silos. Pilgrims travelled to the abandoned remains of Drax where the darkness still breathed softly in the cooling towers.
And in the deep black silence beneath the earth, the Pro Ks continued their endless work.
Consuming. Transforming. Reforming.
Not evil. Never evil.
Simply alive in the only way nature has ever truly respected.
Without guilt. Without mercy. Without end.
The school was open.

Not officially. Officially, the commons closed at ten hundred, and the eco-labs as the sci-labs required supervision after dark. But nobody really cared to ask for them. It wasn’t fun without the teachers or the assistants there, and only the seniors wanted to go there anyway. We just had two years till that. Better not think about that now. I wanted to find Melissi.

I crossed the eastern wing toward the abandoned classrooms; the older concrete block preserved from before the redesigns. Too wasteful to start anew. But I knew. Teachers liked keeping parts of the world intact. They said students needed to remember what people once believed learning looked like: sealed windows, fluorescent lighting, rows of chairs facing authority. I don’t like that. But I kind of liked the way the color mixed with it. It was easier to hide notes away too.
The buildings curved around gardens dense with plants and fruit vines.

Moss climbed the pale walls in deliberate seams. Ventilation shafts breathed cool night air through corridors lined with fig trees growing directly from the architecture. Even after class ends, students wandered quietly between terraces carrying tea or project tablets or blankets over their shoulders.
The room I found still smelled faintly of dust and old paper.
Melisse was inside.
“Aloi Melissi.” I said. She stood near the back cabinets sorting through scattered storage boxes, black hair clipped loosely behind her neck.
Someone had left the windows open and vines had started creeping through the cracked frame years ago.
“You still scavenging?” I asked.
Without turning, she smiled. “Aloi. Historical preservation.”
“That’s what they call stealing now?”
She held up a handful of old projector disks triumphantly.
I leaned against the doorway.
“You want to watch something?”
That made her pause.
Outside, the campus lights dimmed automatically into their night cycle, amber pathways glowing softly beneath the trees.
“What?”
“Tron.”
She stared for a second.
“The old one?”
“The very old one.”
“That’s terrible.”
“Exactly.”

We hurriedly carried chairs into the central commons; the wide circular atrium students called the Lights Place because of the suspended algae lanterns drifting overhead like floating moons. We dragged an old medium-screen display from storage and set it crookedly between two planter walls while the system projected artificial stars across the glass ceiling.
By the time the movie started, half the campus sounded asleep.
Then her roommate arrived. “Aloi.” We said.
He wandered in wearing oversized grey sleep clothes, blond hair flattened on one side. Melisse looked over immediately.
“You alive?”
“Debatable.”
“You slept yet?”
“I don’t sleep.”
“Lie.”
A pause. He’s funny, he’s flushing.
“…I sleep strategically.”
He dropped bonelessly beside us anyway.

At some point during the film he ended up half across my lap, enormous and warm like some exhausted animal pretending not to be tired. Nobody commented on it except Valery when she arrived carrying steaming cups of herbal tea.
She stopped mid-step.
“Why,” she asked carefully, “do you have a giant bear on you?”
I looked down.
He lifted one hand weakly without opening his eyes.
“Structural support,” he muttered.
Melisse started laughing so hard she nearly spilled her drink.
The movie flickered blue light across all of us while outside the mushroom walls breathed cool oxygen into the night air, and for a while nobody spoke anymore.
I rested my head back and watched the city glow through the trees beyond the glass.
Everything felt strangely gentle.

Somehow, he moved a hand towards me, slightly touching the edges of my shirt. I noticed we bought the same brand. I want to ask him if got the fabrics from there and made it himself or if he bought ones of the premade ones. But I bet he hasn’t. Nobody really bought the premade ones, who would?
He softly looks at me then. Drats and crumbles, have I been staring at him?

I bet not. I hope not. Has anybody noticed? I don’t think they have. Melissi is clinging to Val while we watched a man get rescued by a cat. I have completely lost the plot. But I didn’t care. All I wanted was to know more of him. Did he aloi purple-bops? Is his hair naturally blonde? Does he know his eyes shine? What was he going to do later? Maybe we were going to the same career and we didn’t know. Would we be business friends?
As if the world had finally decided enough was enough, the movie ended.
We packed the chairs away together while the last credits rolled silently across the screen. Outside, the air smelled faintly of wet leaves and rooftop gardens.

Valery took my arm and Melissi’s and proclaimed how old movies were really hard to get. We just laughed. Melissi of course started to debate with her, but I couldn’t really tell her anything, all I wanted to do was take his hand.
“You should defend me! Valery is winning!”
“Eh?” I try to come up with something. “Well, the movie was kind of difficult to understand this time.”

“What’s hard to get about it?! It’s clear that cats were far more intelligent even then than they gave them credit for! Honestly, that’s why I’m going into species history. Of course, insensible gals like you were going to eco-eng.”
“You’re going to eco-eng too?” He said. Oh boy, please let me not blush.
“I mean, is there any other career that’s as beautiful as eco-eng?”
He laughs. He thinks I’m funny.
“Come on!”
“We sure love your passion Melissi, but ours is the career of the future! Say, they are trying to make a compound that solely depends on mushrooms.
No water needed!”
“That’s impossible!”
“You bet I want to be on that team. And once I’m there, you’re going to see my name on the holigrams all over the city!”

We laughed harder this time. It’s true that they are trying everything nowadays. I can only hope to be posted on a good department here in my city. I looked around, the towers breathed with gardens climbing their sides in luminous green spirals, filtering heat and rainwater through living membranes. And somewhere below us, the night trams moved soundlessly between districts. How could I ever leave?

“Well, it has been fun.” Valery lived in the cooperative terraces near the southern water canals. My mom’s grandma lived here. I used to visit and help on their shared kitchens or energy systems. I met her there. Unruly, almost always getting me into trouble. But gran helped us fix it anyway.

Now that she’s not there, we changed the kitchens with childcare. I think Valery liked that more than fixing tubes and props. But I am not really going to say anything. She has decided long ago she wanted to do something better. “Do your parents know you want to move two whole cities down?” Melissi asked her.
“They do. I am going to take the test this summer. You know, its still a meritocracy there. But its me, so you don’t have nothing to worry about.”
“It had to be you.”
“If you abandon eco-eng for cat archaeology, I will sue you.”
“Species history,” Melissi corrected with dignity.
“Easy science.”
“You wound me.” They hugged. I couldn’t help but compare them to two flicks of fire whenever they did that. It was funny.
“You know my pops can help you study for the test. He’s in there.”

“Oh, I knew you have been waiting for me to ask you. But I want to start this alone.” I looked at them, wondering when have they met before? But it probably was thanks to Melissi. “But I will ask eventually!” She laughs.
I went in for a hug then, because I aloi Valory. I don’t want her to go so far away. I understand that she needs to do this. And I am of no real help to her, not like him or like Melissi.
But still, “Valory I want you to know that, even if you are here or anywhere, you can always count on us to help you. I bet you will do it!”
She looks at me, silent, then she hugs me back. I am going to miss Valory.

Melissi’s residential tower had been grown around preserved ruins from the old financial district, glass and ivy wrapped together like two centuries forced to coexist. She had put on curtains to help with the view, because the glass sometimes broke at storms, and nets were necessary to put on the sidelines. She knows I hate the sole look of it. I told her to move already, but she refuses to. She had put a lot of effort on the place. And honestly, it looked good from the inside. Her parents actually loved the idea of glass integration in residential ecosystems and worked on a program focused almost entirely on that. I didn’t understand most of it, but I knew Melissi never wanted to join them. So, species history. Good thing is our university offers both careers so its only a matter of time before we both move to campus and begin our fun-filled adventure stories, like those on the graphic novels. And now, him too.
““You guys want tea?” Melissi asked while unlocking the inner door.
“Always.”

The apartment brightened softly as we stepped inside. Living walls lined the curved hallway, threaded with tiny white nylon fibers in the shapes of little cats and insects. We waited there while she brew the water. I automatically looked to the window, watching the city glow a pale blue-green, and wondering if my parents had arrived home already.

Anything other than look to him. Melissi’s place always felt strangely transparent, like living inside a greenhouse suspended above the world. I loved it. But every single time we had exams and we came here to study it never failed to make me sick. I bet it’s the windows. And now it’s making me sick again.
“No! My parents are calling,” she groaned suddenly, checking her wrist display. “If I disappear for twenty minutes, assume I’ve been recruited into architectural propaganda.”
“We’ll remember you fondly.”
She pointed accusingly at him before disappearing down the corridor.
Which somehow left me alone with him. Dangerous. Real dangerous.
I hurry to the kitchen for that tea, him following behind me. “Do you want anything with it? Melissi has honey.”
“I’d take some milk with it.”
“Milk? But Melissi doesn’t buy milk, we would need to order it-” I forgot. He laughed at me. Right. He lives here too.

All too sudden, he was besides me, opening a cute bunny can on the side of Melissi’s clips of our favourite movie scenes. I tried to distract myself by pouring me plain water. Honey would not help me now.

When I came to the living room, I noticed he had settled near the window, stretched sideways across the long sofa like gravity affected him differently than everyone else. Up close, I noticed things I hadn’t before.
His hair really was naturally blond.

Not the polished gold you saw in advertisements or old entertainment archives, but softer, uneven in places, still flattened from sleep near the back. One sleeve had slipped down his arm slightly, exposing faint green ink lines across his wrist—botanical drafting marks, maybe.
Eco-eng. Of course.
His room partition stood partially open from where I sat.
I tried not to stare.
Failed perfectly.
“You want to see my room?” I said nothing.

He smiled and told me to follow him. Flowery cups left messily on the floor, half drunk. The space looked surprisingly organized for someone who claimed not to sleep. Hanging moss lamps casted a warm, greenish light over stacked design tablets and half-disassembled orchydeas spread across the desk. One wall displayed projected ecosystem maps shifting slowly between wetland simulations and fungal root structures. And birds.
Lots of birds.
He noticed me looking. Again. Of course.
“It’s messy.”
“This is your version of messy?”
“You should see it during exams.”
I laughed softly before I could stop myself.
“Why birds?”
“Why not?”
So quick. “Well, you’re into eco-eng,” clearly, “so why birds?”
“Do you know that birds are actually studied for the trams?” Well yes.
“Their perfect anatomy allows them to dive down without as much as a peek. Or to stay suspended on the air for hours.”
I don’t follow it. “Wouldn’t that be transport?”

He laughs. “Melissi was right about you. You’re blunt. But I like it. I think its cute.” Oh, I am definitely blushing now. He takes a toy of a hummingbird and traces its wings. “I want to create cities that would not depend on the ground to stand up.”
What? “You mean, suspencion?”
“Yes. I aloi birds. I want to co-exist with them too. But I can’t go further up.

Look at this place. Many of them died there because they couldn’t see the glass,” that’s true, “I want to be able to live with them. Share my home with them. And there’s a new club that wants the same things that I do.”
Wow. I think, I think- “I think that is awesome.” I think that he’s awesome.
For a moment neither of us spoke.
Outside the glass walls, the city lights pulsed gently through the vertical gardens while somewhere below a night tram slipped soundlessly through the lower districts.
He tilted his head toward me slightly.
“You really aloi eco-eng that much?”
I think that was the moment I truly did.

Before I could answer him properly, Melissi ran dramatically from the hallway, collapsing against his doorway. “They want to add reflective algae panels to residential bridges now,” she announced. “My mother used the phrase light ecology fourteen times.”

And as if from a dream, I felt awake. The hour had grown late without any of us noticing. I knew by now the rooftop gardens I had to tend to would have folded their night petals inward, and my mom would be prepping dinner with my dad. It was time to leave.

Melissi looked at me once, grunted out a “I wish I could’ve spent more time with you”, hugged me and went to retrieve the cups. I half-scream at her back from his room, “We will see each other tomorrow!”
She groans again, making my mood lighter. I suddenly don’t feel as sick anymore. It’s like I’m at peace. Didn’t they say this was supposed to happen after the test? Who knows.
Nobody said anything immediately.
At the entrance, I wrapped myself around Melissi with the emotional violence of somebody incapable of normal affection. She did the same too.
But then she looked toward us both and smiled knowingly enough that I immediately distrusted her.
“Goodnight, future ecosystem legends.”
“That sounds illegal,” he muttered.

She chuckles. We step out into the corridor gardens, thankfully it wasn’t as chilly yet. For a second neither of us moved toward the transit platforms. I still can’t help but wonder how different everything was back them. Yes, it wasn’t perfect. But it was intentional. And maybe that made all the difference.
“Aloi my best friend forever and ever!” Melissi said.
“Aloi to you too, my beautiful Melissi.”
He glanced at me again, tired-eyed and kind of shy in the mosslight.
My chest hurt unexpectedly.
“Aloi, you.” He said softly.
And it was in that moment, that I forgot something completely, totally, dreadfully, embarrassing.
That I had never asked for his name.
“Aloi… you.”
